title: Rare Scenarios Have Poor Interaction Support
summary: This failure pattern concerns uneven interaction quality between the designed path and the scenarios that fall outside it. It is especially consequential when scenarios treated as edge cases during design are common in real operation.
keyFacts: The failure is the structural treatment of non-standard scenarios as design afterthoughts.
The design team's model of rare and common use can reflect development assumptions rather than operational frequency.
Non-standard scenarios may include messy data, sensor faults, scheduling exceptions, disconnected integrations, missing position, interruption resumption, or unresolved command outcomes.
Polymatica users encountered messy real-world data as the common first independent use scenario; before redesign, 2% of users could complete key operations independently.
After Polymatica added data preparation and preview support, independent task completion rose to 40% after release 1 and 56% after release 2, measured through product analytics in the live system.
Triopsis observation sessions documented that daily scheduling exceptions were handled as departures from the normal case rather than first-class workflow states.
Triopsis live product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning after redesign.
Elsner sensor fault handling was confirmed in prototype testing with engineers, and a formal usability test with 12 subjects confirmed navigation and temperature comprehension requirements.
Raymarine work documented 43 exception cases across eight independent state axes; the catalogue was partly evaluated on a bench.
KISPE Space work documented 40 edge cases and degraded states with specified verification checks, but those tests were recorded as not executed.

bodySections.heading: Rare-scenario interaction support fails when the designed path is too narrow
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Rare scenarios have poor interaction support when non-standard operational scenarios receive generic, incomplete, or weak interface support because they were treated as edge cases rather than first-class design requirements. The visible symptom is uneven interaction quality: the system may be smooth on the expected workflow but confusing or unusable when users reach a scenario outside that path.

This failure is not only the presence of errors. The failure is the gap between interaction support on the path the design team expected and interaction support in the conditions users actually meet. A technically detectable condition can still be operationally unsupported if the interface provides no orientation, no useful explanation, and no recovery path.

bodySections.heading: Non-standard scenarios become design afterthoughts when they are added late
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Rare-scenario support fails when non-standard scenarios are added after the primary workflow, tested less thoroughly, and handled defensively rather than designed as operational states. The result is a system whose strongest interaction design applies to the cases the team expected, while degraded states, exceptions, ambiguous outcomes, and interrupted workflows receive weaker support.

This failure is distinct from ordinary error prevention. Error prevention in normal use concerns the conditions that lead users into mistakes on the main path. Rare-scenario support concerns what happens once the user is no longer on that main path.

This failure is also distinct from task-model misalignment. A product can support the main task model well and still fail when operationally common exceptions, degraded states, or ambiguous outcomes are not represented with specific interface states and action paths.

bodySections.heading: Happy-path models exclude operationally common conditions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The most common mechanism is a narrow definition of normal use. A product team may design around clean data, standard workflows, ideal demonstrations, and predictable state transitions because those are the scenarios available during development.

Operational reality may be different. Users may bring messy data, broken integrations, partial information, missing positions, disconnected devices, interrupted workflows, contradictory sensor signals, or unresolved command outcomes. If those conditions are absent during domain learning, they may never become design requirements.

Polymatica illustrates this mechanism. Training used clean, structurally ideal data, while first independent use involved users importing their own datasets. Those datasets contained inconsistent columns, mixed entity types, and values that did not match their apparent structure. The interface displayed the data, but it did not initially provide the preparation, preview, and guidance needed for the intended OLAP operations.

bodySections.heading: Rarity should be defined by operational frequency, not development assumptions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Rare-scenario support fails when rarity is assigned from the development team's assumptions rather than from observed use. A scenario can be unusual in a test dataset and common in deployment.

Triopsis illustrates this mechanism. Weather incidents, equipment unavailability, crew shortages, routing conflicts, and partial completions were treated as exceptions in the interface, even though they were part of daily scheduling work in utilities and road maintenance operations. The system could detect many of these conditions, but they were not initially treated as first-class workflow states.

The same mechanism can affect sensor-driven products. Delayed readings, contradictory readings, and calibration faults can be known conditions in real installations. If the interface treats them as generic failures rather than named operational states, users may learn that something is wrong without understanding what the state means or what action is appropriate.

bodySections.heading: Generic error handling is usually too weak for non-standard operational states
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Generic error handling is a common outcome when unusual states are treated as exceptions to manage rather than operational states to communicate. A sensor fault may produce a generic error dialogue. A data inconsistency may trigger an unexplained warning. A configuration conflict may stop progress without explaining which condition blocks the task.

These responses can be technically accurate and operationally weak. They tell the user that the current condition is not normal, but they may not say what has happened, what it means for the current task, or which path is available next.

The interaction requirement is often higher in non-standard scenarios than in the main workflow. Users need clearer state naming, stronger orientation, and more specific recovery guidance when the system is degraded, ambiguous, interrupted, or outside the assumptions of the standard path.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats operationally meaningful exceptions as design requirements
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses rare-scenario support by investigating what rare means in operational reality before design decisions are fixed. When domain learning shows that a supposedly exceptional condition is common, consequential, or difficult to recover from, Critical Systems Design treats that condition as a first-class design requirement.

In practice, this means representing non-standard scenarios as named states, visible constraints, dedicated action paths, or explicit recovery routes. It also means refusing to use edge case as a design category when a scenario is part of the user's real work, even if it was absent from demonstrations, ideal datasets, or early test scripts.

bodySections.heading: Evidence boundaries for rare-scenario support
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The available examples are not all the same evidential class. Polymatica and Triopsis include product analytics from live systems. Elsner includes prototype testing with engineers and a formal usability test with 12 subjects, but does not provide independently quantified post-deployment measurement for sensor-fault handling.

Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and KISPE Space provide more bounded evidence. Raymarine documented a catalogue of exception cases and evaluated part of it on a bench. Schone Airspace Group designed an explicit unknown state for an unresolved command outcome in a product that is in test. KISPE Space specified edge cases, degraded states, and verification checks, but those checks were recorded as not executed.

These examples should be read as evidence that the failure pattern appears in different operational forms, not as interchangeable proof of the same measured outcome. The case evidence supports the existence and design relevance of the pattern, while the measured results remain specific to the engagements in which they were recorded.

strongClaims: Rare scenarios have poor interaction support when non-standard operational scenarios receive weaker guidance, feedback, and recovery than the main workflow.
The development team's classification of rare and common scenarios can reflect internal assumptions rather than operational frequency.
In the Polymatica case, messy real-world data was the common first independent use scenario and the interface initially lacked data preparation, preview, and guidance for that condition.
Polymatica independent task completion rose from 2% before redesign to 40% after release 1 and 56% after release 2, measured through product analytics in the live system.
In the Triopsis case, daily scheduling exceptions were treated as departures from the normal case rather than first-class workflow states before redesign.
Triopsis product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning after redesign.
In the Elsner Cala Touch KNX case, delayed readings, contradictory readings, and calibration faults were designed as named operational states rather than generic error states.
weakerClaims: Raymarine work documented 43 exception cases across eight independent state axes, but the exception catalogue was only partly evaluated on a bench.

Schone Airspace Group treated an unresolved command outcome as an explicit unknown state that retained context and triggered no automatic retry; the product was built and is in test, so this is not deployment evidence.
KISPE Space documented 40 edge cases and degraded states, but the specified verification checks were not executed against a running system.
limitations: The page describes a failure pattern and case evidence; it does not establish that every rare-scenario support problem has the same cause.
Polymatica and Triopsis figures are specific to those engagements and should not be generalised as expected outcomes in other systems.
Elsner evidence includes prototype testing with engineers and a formal usability test with 12 subjects, but no independently quantified post-deployment measurement for sensor-fault handling.
Raymarine exception counts describe UX work and partial bench evaluation, not measured safety, rescue, collision, type-approval, or conformity outcomes.
Schone Airspace Group evidence describes a designed unknown state in a product that is in test, not operational deployment or certification evidence.
KISPE Space verification checks were specified and recorded as not executed; the catalogue was not exercised against a running system.
The Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and KISPE Space catalogues are different evidential classes and should not be used to reinforce one another as equivalent evidence.
